transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Jin (Redwood PM), Maya (Legato VP Eng), Omar (Legato Platform), Priya (Legato Security), Leo (Legato Infra)

Summary:
Short deep dive on private VPC deployment options for Legato: focus on egress/NAT, AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints, SNI/mTLS termination, and runtime impacts of KV cache + batching. Agreed to run a short benchmark pilot with KV cache warmup and a 20ms batching window. Action items and next steps listed.

Topics covered (auto):
- PrivateLink architecture and cross-account ENI placement
- Egress / NAT behavior and hairpinning concerns for inference calls
- TLS termination, SNI passthrough, and mTLS for logging/metrics backhaul
- KV cache invalidation, TTL, and per-shard memory sizing
- Batching latency/throughput tradeoffs and quantization impacts on latency

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya (Legato): Maya here.
[00:07] Omar (Legato): Omar on platform.
[00:09] Priya (Legato): Priya from security.
[00:12] Samir (Redwood SE): Samir here. Jin's on too.
[00:15] Jin (Redwood PM): hi all.
[00:18] Avery: Great. Our plan is to walk the high-level PrivateLink layout then dig into egress/NAT and KV cache/batching details. We'll call out config knobs and then decide pilot scope.
[00:26] Maya: Sounds good, our main constraints: PHI data can't leave VPC, we need mTLS to third-party observability, and we want p99 under 120ms for chat workloads. Cost is secondary but relevant.
[00:38] Samir: Cool. For PrivateLink on AWS we typically use interface endpoints backed by an NLB in our infra account. That creates ENIs in your selected subnets, so you need to pick subnets across AZs for redundancy.
[00:50] Leo (Legato): Quick q — those ENIs will consume IPs in each subnet, right? We have tight /24s in prod.
[00:55] Samir: Yes, ENIs take IPs. For high-throughput endpoints we recommend 2-3 ENIs per AZ, so recommend at least /22 if you can, otherwise we'll guide a minimal layout.
[01:06] Omar: If we can't enlarge subnets, can we put PrivateLink in a separate management VPC and VPC-peering to app VPC?
[01:12] Samir: You can, but peering plus NAT starts to get complicated. Hairpinning becomes a factor if app instances need to call the endpoint back through the NAT gateway. We usually advise interface endpoints in the same VPC as the callers to avoid hairpin.
[01:24] Priya: On security — how do you handle mTLS and SNI? Our compliance team requires mutual TLS for egress to our observability stack, and key ownership needs to stay with us.
[01:34] Jin: For mTLS we support end-to-end mutual TLS between your sidecar and our service; PrivateLink preserves TLS, so termination happens at your end unless you want Redwood to terminate and re-establish TLS, which we prefer to avoid for PHI.
[01:46] Samir: Just to add — SNI passthrough is supported. If you're doing SNI-based routing in your outbound proxy, make sure the NLB is configured TCP (not TLS) so SNI bytes aren't stripped. Sometimes hosts set the NLB to TLS and that breaks SNI routing.
[01:58] Maya: Good to know. Also, we operate an egress proxy for audit logging. Does Redwood expect direct outbound to telemetry endpoints or can it go via our proxy?
[02:08] Avery: You can route through your egress proxy. Two things to watch: keepalive and idle timeouts on the proxy, and connection reuse. Short keepalives lead to more TLS handshakes which adds latency.
[02:20] Omar: Our current NAT gateway idle timeout kills TCP after 350s, and our proxy terminates idle connections at 60s. Will that affect KV cache and persistent KV connections?
[02:28] Samir: It can. If connections reset frequently, per-request handshake cost increases. For KV-cache we prefer to keep gRPC or HTTP/2 streams open to preserve KV sharding and hot prefix cache warmness. So set idle timeouts to something higher, 10+ minutes, or configure TCP keepalive.
[02:42] Priya: Are there any special ports or protocols we need to open between subnets and endpoints?
[02:46] Samir: Just standard TCP for PrivateLink. For metrics backhaul (Prometheus push or mTLS REST), open outbound to your observability IPs, or route to your proxy. If using mutual auth, ensure your CA certs are loaded in the sidecars.
[02:57] Leo: You mentioned hairpin earlier — can you show an example where hairpin causes p99 spikes?
[03:02] Samir: Sure. If runner instances in same VPC call the interface endpoint and that endpoint routes back through a NAT in the same AZ, you can hit extra hops and SNAT, breaking connection reuse. Example: 1-2 ms extra latency per call becomes 8-12ms at p99 when combined with TLS reconnects. In small windowed workloads that kills p99.
[03:21] Maya: We aim for p95 < 60ms, p99 < 120ms. For chat at 4k context sizes, are those targets realistic with KV cache?
[03:29] Samir: Yes with warmed KV cache. If KV cache hits are high, we can serve many tokens without model recompute. For typical 4k contexts, with a 20ms batching window and max batch=16 our internal runs show p95 around 40-60ms and p99 ~110-140ms depending on token size and quantization.
[03:44] Avery: Important detail — batching window tradeoffs. Short windows (5-10ms) reduce latency but lower throughput efficiency. 20ms is a sweet spot for many chat workloads. If Legato prefers lower p99 we can go 10ms and increase dedicated capacity.
[03:58] Omar: How does quantization affect the runtime latency?
[04:02] Samir: 4-bit quantization (LLM.q4) reduces memory and can slightly speed up token generation on some kernels, but for single-token latency the difference is typically 5-15% depending on hardware. Quantization also impacts throughput — it can increase batch capacity per GPU. However, beware of quality regressions; we'll recommend evals on your prompts.
[04:19] Priya: On KV cache invalidation — if we push model updates or user prompts change schema, how do you recommend TTLs and shard sizes?
[04:27] Samir: We recommend hybrid strategy: short TTL for session-level ephemeral prefixes (30-120s) and longer TTL for shared static prefixes (hours). Per-shard memory sizing depends on model KV footprint; a 7B model's KV per token is small, but for 70B it grows. We'll provide a sizing table in the follow-up.
[04:42] Maya: Can you talk about KV warmup during failover? If a node restarts how long to reach steady-state p95?
[04:49] Samir: Warmup time depends on traffic locality and cache replication. If you have steady traffic, warmup to 80% effective hit-rate can be minutes. We do cross-shard replication for hot prefixes in Dedicated, and you can pre-warm by replaying recent requests. We'll provide scripts to seed cache for pilot.
[05:05] Leo: Regarding networking, any recommendations on subnet sizing for ENIs and NAT throughput?
[05:09] Samir: For production, each interface endpoint will scale ENIs with traffic; provision /22 per AZ if possible. For NAT throughput, use NAT Gateway with autoscale and ensure you have enough elastic IPs. If you see SNAT port exhaustion, we'll provide metrics queries to detect it.
[05:23] Jin: Let's jump to an example pilot config we propose: PrivateLink interface endpoints in two AZs, 2 subnets each, NAT only for non-inference egress, direct interface endpoints for inference, keepalive 600s, batching window 20ms, max batch 16, kvcache TTL session 60s. Run 1-hour synthetic traffic to measure p50/p95/p99 and token cost.
[05:45] Maya: That looks fine; we need mTLS to our Splunk stack for logs and we need keys to remain in our KMS. How does Redwood integrate with customer KMS?
[05:54] Avery: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS via our keywrap flow: you keep the CMK and we wrap ephemeral keys. For the hosted path we can also accept encrypted payloads. We'll send the KMS integration doc.
[06:04] Priya: Are audit logs available for model inputs/outputs? Our policy allows storing metadata only.
[06:09] Samir: Yes — Redwood Private can be configured to only log metadata or redact payloads. We can export audit logs to your S3 or SIEM via our sidecar. Note: ensure your VPC egress rules allow S3 endpoints if you want direct delivery.
[06:20] Maya: Back to performance: what about DNS resolution and resolver caching? We saw spikes when our resolver had high latencies.
[06:28] Samir: DNS can definitely add tens of ms. For PrivateLink, use VPC interface endpoints for S3 and other services to avoid public resolver hops. Also, run a local DNS cache on nodes (e.g., systemd-resolved or dnsmasq) to avoid repeated queries.
[06:41] Omar: Any special flags on the Redwood runtime for hairpin detection?
[06:45] Samir: We have instrumented headers to detect hops and will report when hairpin is present. For the pilot, we'll enable detailed tracing to surface extra RTTs.
[06:52] Maya: Let's talk about observability — we want per-request tracing and cost breakdowns. Can you push traces to our agent?
[06:58] Jin: Yes, we can push OpenTelemetry spans to your OTLP endpoint over mTLS. The sidecar will aggregate token-level timings and cost estimates per request.
[07:07] Priya: Any legal constraints around data residency if the control plane is in our account but logs route to a different region?
[07:12] Avery: You can pin log export regionally. For Private deployments the control plane can be in your VPC or in our infra with strict data residency bindings; we have options and contracts for that.
[07:22] Maya: For the pilot, we prefer the control plane in our VPC. Cost and team bandwidth are considerations.
[07:26] Avery: Noted. We'll propose the Private control plane deployment steps in the follow-up.
[07:31] Omar: A couple more nitty gritty items — TCP keepalive frequency, maximum concurrent streams per node, and gRPC window sizes. Any defaults?
[07:38] Samir: Defaults we use: TCP keepalive at 300s, but recommend 600s for your proxy; gRPC max concurrent streams default 100, but we can tune up to 1k per process for high concurrency. gRPC window sizes we leave default but can increase for large-batch responses. We'll share sample sysctl and sidecar configs.
[07:54] Leo: Regarding cost, if we go with dedicated capacity vs hosted, how much does batching move the cost per token?
[07:59] Jin: Batching increases throughput and amortizes GPU cost. Typical savings are 20-40% depending on batch size and quantization. We'll run your workload in the pilot to produce a more precise number.
[08:12] Maya: OK — can we go through an example request path end-to-end?
[08:15] Samir: Sure. Caller (app pod) -> local sidecar -> local DNS to resolve endpoint -> interface endpoint ENI (PrivateLink) -> Redwood NLB -> Redwood inference node. For telemetry: sidecar -> your observability proxy (mTLS) -> Splunk. For egress to external token services, go through NAT if needed. If any of those hops close connections, you pay handshake cost.
[08:35] Omar: If we have an internal API gateway that does SNI routing, we need the SNI preserved. Confirmed earlier that TCP NLB retains SNI?
[08:42] Samir: Right, use TCP not TLS for NLB listeners to pass SNI bytes. If you need listener-level TLS for cert management, you can terminate TLS on the gateway but then you'd need to re-establish mTLS to Redwood which we prefer to avoid for PHI.
[08:54] Maya: Understood. A small concern: our infra team saw occasional DNS TTLs at 0 causing flapping. Is there any defensive strategy on the Redwood side?
[09:01] Samir: We do client-side caching in the sidecar and also use connection pooling, so momentary DNS blips shouldn't drop in-flight requests. We'll also instrument more aggressive retry/backoff to smooth transient DNS issues.
[09:14] Maya: Great. Any notes about SNI and ALPN for http2?
[09:18] Samir: ALPN negotiation for h2 is fine. For SNI, ensure client sends the host header and SNI; certain proxies strip it. We'll flag if we detect missing SNI in the pilot traces.
[09:28] Priya: One compliance question — if we keep keys, who manages rotation?
[09:31] Avery: You manage CMK rotation; we support periodic re-wrap. We can run key rotation drills with you.
[09:36] Omar: Let's capture pilot milestones: 1) network diagram and subnet CIDRs, 2) sidecar + keepalive config, 3) seed KV cache + run scripted load, 4) collect p50/p95/p99 and token costs.
[09:47] Jin: We'll propose a one-week pilot timeline: 2 days for infra setup, 1 day for config validation, 1 day for run and 1 day for analysis.
[09:56] Maya: Acceptable. One more: our compliance needs audit-level proof of TLS parameters and cipher suites.
[10:01] Priya: yes.
[10:02] Samir: We'll include cipher suite matrix in the security checklist. For mTLS we recommend ECDHE with AES-GCM and TLS1.3.
[10:10] Maya: Perfect.
[10:12] Avery: Quick recap of next steps: Avery sends PrivateLink diagram and security checklist; Samir shares kvcache sample and batching script; Omar shares CIDRs and proxy timeouts. We'll aim to start the pilot 2026-10-13.
[10:22] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:24] [meeting wrap + small crosstalk]
